# Homothetic fibers: a quantitative Jensen-core theorem and a projective obstruction

The general bound Gamma_d/h(P) for arbitrary compatible homothetic
fibers is not established here. This note proves an explicit sufficient
condition allowing non-Jensen translations, and gives a compatible
four-disk family for which neither a common marked point nor a
base-denominator projective chart removes the translation defect.

The projective transport issues in `candidate 7bd76540986ac981`
and the contact-mass restriction in
`candidate 8c2b392c7a2005ed` remain in force.
No unweighted projective depth assertion is invoked.

## 1. Exact compatibility slack for homothetic fibers

Let K be a full-dimensional compact convex body in R^d, d>=1. Let
P be a nonempty finite lattice-convex subset of Z^n, and suppose
the actual positive fibers are

    K_p=c_p+r_p K,                 r_p>0.                (1)

For an anchored representation j=sum_i lambda_i p_i, define

    R=sum_i lambda_i r_(p_i),
    delta=r_j-R,
    Delta=sum_i lambda_i c_(p_i)-c_j.

Then the corresponding compatibility inclusion holds IF AND ONLY IF

    delta>=0,             Delta in delta K,              (2)

where 0K={0}. Indeed the Minkowski average is
sum_i lambda_i c_(p_i)+R K. Its containment in c_j+r_j K is
equivalent, by support functions, to

    v dot Delta <= delta h_K(v)  for every v.

Adding the inequalities for v and -v and using positive width of
K forces delta>=0. For delta>0 the remaining inequalities are
exactly membership in delta K; for delta=0 they force Delta=0.

Thus zero radius surplus forces exact Jensen affinity of the
centers in that relation. Positive surplus permits a genuine
translation defect. These are all anchored relations, not only
midpoints of neighboring indices.

## 2. A quantitative theorem from an ordinary depth margin

Fix t in int K, and let beta be its ordinary normalized halfspace
depth in the uniform body K. Put

    J=K-t,             b_p=c_p+r_p t.

Then 0 is interior to J, beta is its ordinary depth at zero, and
K_p=b_p+r_p J. Let gauge_J(v)=inf{a>=0:v in aJ} be its possibly
asymmetric Minkowski gauge. Write L(P) for the scalar functions
preserving every anchored convex representation in P.

For ANY vector-valued a in L(P) tensor R^d, define

    q_p=(r_p-gauge_J(a_p-b_p))_+.

Let h=h(P), let M=|K| sum_p r_p^d be the original mixed mass, and
let D_max be maximum normalized original mixed depth. Then

    D_max >= [beta/h] [sum_p q_p^d / sum_p r_p^d].        (3)

This is a proved bound with a deterministic actual center. It does
not assume that an arbitrary directional law comes from one measure.

For q_p>0, gauge membership and convexity give the actual inclusion

    a_p+q_p J subset b_p+r_p J=K_p.                     (4)

Only these positive cores are used. If q_p=0 and a_p lies outside
K_p, the singleton {a_p} is NOT declared to be an inner subbody.

Let E={p:q_p>0}. If it is empty, (3) is the trivial zero bound.
Otherwise put P_E=conv(E) intersect P. Since P is lattice-convex,
P_E is the full integer set in conv(E). Every a_j, j in P_E, is
an actual feasible point: represent j by points of E; Jensen
affinity gives a_j as their convex combination, and (4) plus
convexity of the original body gives (j,a_j) in that body.

The graph hull G=conv{(p,a_p):p in E} has exactly one point over
every integer base j in P_E, namely (j,a_j). Therefore the graph
source T_E has Helly number at most h(P_E), by projecting convex
intersections with G to their base and using the uniqueness of
each integer graph section. Also h(P_E)<=h(P): intersecting a
finite source with a convex set cannot increase its Helly number,
as one can append that fixed convex set to any infeasible family.

Put atomic mass q_p^d at graph point (p,a_p), p in E, and zero
at the other points of T_E. Weighted relative Helly supplies a
point y in T_E for which every containing closed halfspace contains
at least (sum_p q_p^d)/h atomic mass. For clarity, take all closed
halfspaces with atomic mass greater than (1-1/h) of the total.
Any h have a common graph point by the union bound; graph Helly
and finiteness give a common point of the whole family. A cap
through that point with mass less than 1/h would have an open
complement with excessive mass. Moving its boundary slightly
into that complement retains all those finitely many atoms in a
closed halfspace and contradicts the selection. Thus atoms on
boundaries are included correctly.

Whenever a containing original cap includes (p,a_p), its restriction
to the core (4) contains the depth-beta point a_p. It captures at
least beta q_p^d |K| from that core; a constant restriction captures
the whole core. Summing over the captured graph points proves (3).
The selected center lies in the actual original source even when
its own q_j is zero, by the feasibility argument above.

## 3. An explicit non-Jensen regime with the full target

If there is a in L(P) tensor R^d satisfying

    gauge_J(a_p-b_p) <= epsilon r_p for all p,
    0<=epsilon<1,

then (3) gives

    D_max >= beta(1-epsilon)^d/h(P).                    (5)

In particular the full Gamma_d/h(P) target follows whenever

    epsilon <= 1-(Gamma_d/beta)^(1/d).                 (6)

For centrally symmetric K, take its symmetry center t and beta=1/2.
For d>=2 this gives a strictly positive explicit defect tolerance.
More generally, the proved ordinary rigidity theorem
`candidate e2c55c91458e1e8c` says that a
nonsimplex body has ordinary maximal depth beta>Gamma_d, yielding
a positive tolerance at a deepest point. That point is interior:
boundary points have ordinary depth zero. The simplex case has no
positive tolerance from this argument, because its maximal beta is
exactly Gamma_d.

The finite-dimensional tolerance test itself is attained. For fixed
t, minimize max_p gauge_J(a_p-b_p)/r_p over a in L(P) tensor R^d.
The gauge is continuous and comparable to Euclidean norm because
0 is interior to the bounded J. The maximum over the finitely many
coordinates is therefore coercive on that linear subspace. A
minimizer exists. This supplies a concrete convex feasibility test,
not a claim that (6) automatically holds for all compatible families.

## 4. A genuinely non-Jensen four-disk example

Take P={0,1,2,3}, K the unit Euclidean disk in R^2, and

    (r_0,r_1,r_2,r_3)=(1,2,2,1),
    c_0=c_3=0, c_1=(1/10,0), c_2=(0,1/10).             (7)

These are actual compatible fibers of a full convex body. To see
this over ALL real base coordinates, interpolate c and r linearly
between the integers. For a continuous normal v, the fiber support
function is v dot c(z)+r(z)|v|. Its discrete concavity surplus at
either interior integer is at least

    [1/2-sqrt(5)/20]|v|>0.

Hence its piecewise-linear interpolation is concave on [0,3] for
every v. The support-function inclusion criterion makes the union
of these disk fibers a convex compact body with the exact four
integer slices (7). Positive radii give full ambient dimension.

Use t=0, beta=1/2 and the Jensen-affine graph a_p=0. Its core radii
are exactly (1,19/10,19/10,1). Since h(P)=2, (3) yields

    D_max >= (1/4) (461/50)/10 =461/2000 >2/9.           (8)

The last number 2/9 is Gamma_2/h(P). Both bases 1 and 2 are weighted
medians of these core graph masses, so the explicit actual points
(1,0,0) and (2,0,0) each have the guarantee (8). The excess in the
bound is exactly 149/18000. No numerical cap minimization is used.

These translations are not Jensen-affine. In fact no SINGLE marked
point t of the common disk, or even of R^2, makes c_p+r_p t a
Jensen-affine graph. The two interior midpoint equations would
respectively require

    t=(-1/5,1/10),       t=(1/10,-1/5),

which are different. Thus (8) genuinely uses inner cores with
different relative marked points; it is not the trivial exact
singleton-centroid-graph case in another parametrization.

## 5. Base-denominator projective maps preserve the defect

Let ell be affine and strictly positive on the relevant base hull,
and consider an invertible full projective chart

    (p,x) -> (p/ell(p),x/ell(p)).

Translate the base origin first if necessary to ensure the nonzero
constant term required for invertibility. On each fiber this is
a positive homothety, so it sends the centroid to its divided
centroid and likewise sends a marked point b_p to b_p/ell(p).

An original relation j=sum_i lambda_i p_i becomes a relation of
the transformed bases with weights

    theta_i=lambda_i ell(p_i)/ell(j).

The transformed marked-point Jensen identity is equivalent to

    b_j/ell(j)=sum_i theta_i b_(p_i)/ell(p_i)
       iff b_j=sum_i lambda_i b_(p_i).                  (9)

Conversely every transformed relation pulls back to such an
original relation, by the inverse positive chart. Thus Jensen
affinity of the marked graph is invariant under this class of
projective changes. The example (7) cannot be converted to the
trivial marked-graph case by such a map, even after choosing any
common marked point t. The affine base/continuous shears normally
used before these charts also preserve vanishing of the Jensen
defect: their invertible continuous linear part simply multiplies
the old residual vector.

This is an exact obstruction to that proposed simplification, not
to the bound Gamma_d/h(P) itself. Arbitrary large translation
defects and the common-simplex case remain outside the positive
tolerance theorem above.
